alternative: Compile-time templates with a typed context (askama) or typed builder macros (maud, html!), with the model passed as a struct - keep a runtime engine (tera) only where templates must be editable after the build.
idiom_name: askama compile-time templates / maud macro builders over a typed context struct
implementation_notes: Rust has no runtime template scripting in its core and its ecosystem does not want one: a string template with dynamic evaluation fights both the type system and the ownership model, and an untyped context map - the thing a scriptlet engine depends on - is exactly what Rust programs avoid. The native answer is compile-time: askama derives a Template implementation for a struct or enum, turning the template into code with auto-escaping that a malicious value cannot disable, maud builds markup through macros, and tera remains the runtime escape route when templates must change without a rebuild. The classic scriptlet form is justified only in that last case, and even then the context stays typed.
pitfalls: Choosing a runtime engine (tera, handlebars) gives up the compile-time check: a misspelled field becomes a render-time error, which is the failure mode askama exists to eliminate.
The template's context type and the template text must stay in sync; askama enforces it at compile time, a runtime engine only when the page is requested.
Marking a value as safe (a raw/safe filter or equivalent) disables the escaping askama applies by default and reopens the injection path.
Macro builders such as maud make markup a compile-time expression tree - safe and fast, but compile times grow and non-developers can no longer edit the markup.
